title: Efficient Pre-Training with Token Superposition
claim: Our method reaches the same training loss as the baseline in far fewer steps, giving a large equal-compute speedup.
layout: 1 panel, line plot, annotation arrows, orange speedup arrow along bottom
description: A single line chart of training loss (y-axis, roughly 2.2 to 7.5) against training steps (x-axis, 0 to about 120,000). The red Baseline curve drops steeply and then declines slowly, ending near 2.25 at about 123k steps. The blue TST curve starts high and plateaus near 6.1 until about 12k steps. A grey curved arrow labeled 'Return to baseline regime' points at that point, where the curve falls sharply. It then crosses below the baseline and ends at the same loss at about 50k steps. A large bold orange arrow and the label '2.5x speedup' run from the baseline's endpoint back to the TST endpoint. The legend is at top right. The orange annotation draws the eye first.
caption: Loss curves during the pre-training of two Qwen3-like MoE models (10B-A1B) with baseline pretraining and token superposition training (TST) where we stop the training early to match an equal training loss. The baseline training sees 1.05T tokens while the TST training sees 2T data tokens. Every step in all conditions are equal-FLOPs, thus the speedup can be directly computed w.r.t. the number of steps. More details are in Table [ref].
abstract: Pre-training of Large Language Models is often prohibitively expensive and inefficient at scale, requiring complex and invasive modifications in order to achieve high data throughput. In this work, we present Token-Superposition Training (TST), a simple drop-in method that significantly improves the data throughput per FLOPs during pre-training without modifying the parallelism, optimizer, tokenizer, data, or model architecture. TST is done in two phases: (i) A highly efficient superposition phase where we combine many contiguous tokens into one bag and train using a multi-hot cross-entropy (MCE) objective, and (ii) a recovery phase where we revert back to standard training. We extensively evaluate TST on the scale of 270M and 600M parameters and validate on 3B and a 10B A1B mixture of experts model, demonstrating that it is highly robust in different settings. Ultimately, TST consistently outperforms baseline loss and downstream evaluations, and under equal-loss settings, TST yields up to a 2.5x reduction in total pre-training time at the 10B A1B scale.
